Simple Present Tense in Affirmative Statements
You use simple present tense in affirmative statements to describe actions that are true, normal or regular.

You can use simple present tense in affirmative statements to describe object oriented class diagrams.

You just need to follow this grammatical structure:

Subject + Verb + Complement


Example:
Class diagrams organize many different types of information.

* Don't forget to conjugate verbs for third person accordingly.
A class is a design that describes the components of a software system.
UML allows us to suppress any idea we consider irrelevant so the diagram can be clear and understandable.
Class diagram uses (+) for public access and (-) for private access.

Verbs with Infinitives, Need to, in Affirmative and Negative Statements
You use verb+ infinitive in affirmative and negative statements with ‘need to', to express necessity for something.

You use the following structure when writing a verb + infinitive in affirmative statements with “need to”.

Subject + Need + to + Main verb in base form + Complement

Example:
I need to describe a class diagram.

You can also use verbs with infinitives in negative statements by adding the auxiliaries don't or doesn't respectively.

Subject +don't /doesn't + Need + to + Main verb in base form + Complement

Examples:
I don't need to describe a class diagram.
He doesn't need to describe a class diagram.

Other kinds of verbs + infinitives are have to and want to.
You need to use a class diagram to represent any kind of information you want to organize.
If you need to draw a class diagram you don't need to make all information visible.
You need to specify the type of visibility you want for your diagram, but you don't need to use all of them at the same time.
The box structure doesn't need to be complex, but it has some specification you have to follow, such as the elements of a class diagram.
Basic class diagrams are useful to represent specific components within one same category.

When drawing a basic class diagram, UML allows us to suppress irrelevant information in diagrams.

You need to choose an attribute of the category you want to work on. For example, a Class Software with design attributes and with some methods like life cycle, programming language, network protocols, and software samples.

Don't forget that you can use some diagram conventions to clarify your diagram:

+ Public
# Protected
- Private

images.text: Professor Smith: A class is a design that describes the components of a software system. You need to use a class diagram to represent any kind of information that you want to organize. A UML class diagram shows multiple classes in detail and relates them to each other. A class diagram also shows the software architecture of a system, and you need to represent that architecture in a diagram.

If you need to draw a class diagram, you don't need to make all information visible. A UML allows us to suppress any idea that we consider irrelevant, so the diagram can be clear and understandable. You need to clarify the class that you want to organize, but you don't need to organize it before creating a box structure. The box structure doesn't need to be complex, but it has some specifications that you have to follow, like the elements of a class diagram. These elements are first, the class name that has to be unique. Second, the list of attributes that you need to describe the class. And third, a list of methods or operations that you need to follow for a UML class.

Attributes and methods use some modifiers and diagram conventions that differentiate one from another. A class diagram uses (+) for public access and (-) for private access. Attributes are normally private and methods are normally public. You need to specify the type of visibility you want for your diagram, but you don't need to use all of them at the same time. Don't forget that you can use keywords to create your class diagram. Now, it's your turn, according to what you learned today, you need to write a short text explaining how to draw a basic class diagram. You can start right now!
